vulns.description: Certifi versions before 2026.10.18 include the `emSign ECC Root CA - G3` root certificate in their bundled CA store. Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates that chain to this root have compromised private keys and the CA has revoked them.   An attacker with one of the compromised keys can issue valid-looking certificates for any hostname. If the attacker is also on-path, they can intercept or modify TLS traffic from clients that trust the certifi bundle. Examples include `requests`, `urllib3` and `pip`, and the Python.org macOS installer.  Certifi 2026.10.18 removed all emSign roots from the bundle. Certifi 2026.10.19 restored the emSign roots that are not affected. Upgrade to 2026.10.19 or later, and rebuild container images that vendor certifi.

`SoftFileLock` and `MarkerSoftFileLock` evict an unparsable marker (the lock file at `<path>`, whose presence says a process holds the lock) once a waiting contender has watched it unchanged for two seconds. `SoftFileLease` expires a lease the same way. The watch tells two looks apart by the marker's modification time (mtime) and inode number (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) alone.  Another local user (the other user below) who can create files in the lock's directory, a sticky `/tmp` included (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove it), parks an empty file of its own at the lock path. It dates that file to a future tick of the kernel's coarse clock (a clock that advances in steps of 4 ms), lets the waiters of the user running the lock (the lock user below) watch it past two seconds, and unlinks it in that tick. On a filesystem that hands a freed inode number straight back (ext4, overlayfs on ext4) the lock user's next marker repeats both values. It inherits the time spent watching the other user's file, and a second waiter removes it while its owner holds the lock.  Two of the lock user's processes then run the critical section together with no error. A `SoftFileLease` waiter takes a live lease that its owner wrote moments before, within milliseconds instead of after `lease_duration`. Affected versions: filelock >= 4.1.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-RKC48J5B`).  ## Severity  **CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N, 4.7 (Medium).**  `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): a race the other user cannot steer. It needs ext4-style inode reuse, a coarse-clock timestamp tick the other user can predict, and two polls of the lock user inside a 4 ms tick and a ~75 µs create-to-write gap. The scanner measured 2 to 10 % of attempts; none of our own 250 attempts fired. `PR:L` (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the lock user's processes act on their own. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user reads nothing. `I:H` (high integrity impact): two holders write the data the lock protects, and neither learns of the other. `A:N` (no availability impact): the lock keeps working.  Classification from the review: security, conditional, by mechanism. It is the same cross-UID primitive (a UID is a user account's numeric id) as the stale-break inode-reuse race reported in a separate advisory: an inode number reused after the other user's unlink in a sticky directory, which our review reproduced across UIDs, plus a forged future mtime. The scanner rated it high (CWE-694) and demonstrated it across UIDs in its own runs. It did not fire in 250 attempts of ours over ext4 with inode reuse confirmed, nor in the scanner-side triage, so its cross-user claim rests on the report's own runs and on the mechanism.  ## Scope and preconditions  - The other user can create files in the lock's directory; a root-owned `1777` directory is enough. It creates, `utime`s (sets the timestamps of) and unlinks only its own file. In the sticky directory its `unlink`, `rename`, `open(..., "w")` and `utime` on a marker of the lock user all fail, and deleting its own file only frees the lock. - The directory is on a filesystem that reuses a freed inode number at once: ext4, and overlayfs on it (thousands of create/unlink cycles returned one number). tmpfs does not reuse one, so the pair cannot repeat there; btrfs does not either. - File timestamps come from a coarse clock whose future values the other user can compute (`CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE`, 4 ms steps on Linux 6.1; 20,000 file creations all carried that clock's value). - At least two processes of the lock user are waiting on the lock while the other user's file is there. The other user does not choose which processes overlap or when; each attempt blocks the lock for 2.2 s (for a lease, `lease_duration`). - No symbolic link, hard link or FIFO takes part, so the `fs.protected_*` sysctls (Linux settings that restrict following links and opening pipes in sticky world-writable directories) play no part. `StrictSoftFileLock` keys its watch the same way but only raises `SoftFileLockProtocolError`, so it breaks no lock there.  filelock's checks against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.  ## Affected code  At the scanned commit b831496, the watch is [`SoftFileLock._marker_unchanged_for`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L125-L132), with its caller in [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123). The [`MarkerSoftFileLock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_marker.py#L74-L81) and [`SoftFileLease`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_lease.py#L229-L256) paths hand an unparsable marker to the same code. The re-check in [`break_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_util.py#L113-L118) compares the values the contender just read.  ## Introduced  0f7c4d3794dc ("fix(soft): expire leases on the contender's clock", #796, 2026-10-07), first released in 4.1.0 (verified against the tags). Earlier releases compared the marker's mtime with the wall clock, and this does not affect them.  ## Mechanism  `SoftFileLock._acquire` creates the marker with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` (create the file, fail if it exists) and only then writes the holder record. In between it calls `fstat` and `uname`, stats `/proc/self/ns/pid` and reads `/proc/<pid>/stat`, so for about 75 µs (measured) the marker exists and is empty. A contender that polls in that gap must not take the marker for garbage, and the check that protects it is the two-second watch. `_try_break_stale_lock` reads the marker, finds no holder, and calls `break_lock_file(lock_file, mtime, ino)` only if `_marker_unchanged_for(mtime, ino)` reaches `MALFORMED_LOCK_AGE_THRESHOLD` (2.0 s). That function keeps `self._marker_seen = ((mtime, ino), first seen)` across polls and returns the elapsed monotonic time (time from a clock that only moves forward) while the pair repeats.  Neither half of the pair belongs to one file. A file's owner sets its mtime to any value with `utime`, a future time included, and ext4 gives the inode number of an unlinked file to the next file created in the directory.  1. While the lock is free, the other user creates an empty file at the lock path (inode `I`) and sets its mtime to `T`, a tick of the coarse clock about 2.2 s in the future. 2. Every waiting process of the lock user polls each 50 ms, reads an empty file and records `_marker_seen = ((T, I), first seen)`. After 2 s each poll calls `break_lock_file`, whose `rename` fails with `EPERM` (operation not permitted; seen with `strace`): the directory is sticky and the file belongs to the other user. `suppress(OSError, ...)` swallows the error, the file stays, and nothing resets `_marker_seen`. 3. When the coarse clock reaches `T`, the other user unlinks its file. Inode `I` is free. 4. Process F of the lock user polls during tick `T`. Its `O_EXCL` create succeeds, and its marker is inode `I` with mtime `T`. 5. Process S polls before F has written its record. It reads an empty file with pair `(T, I)`, `_marker_unchanged_for` returns the 2.2 s that S spent watching the other user's file, and S calls `break_lock_file(lock_file, T, I)`. 6. `break_lock_file` compares mtime and inode before and after its rename, but with the values S just read from F's marker, so both checks pass. F's marker has S's UID, so the rename and the unlink succeed. 7. F writes its record into the unlinked inode and returns from `acquire()`. The path is empty, so the next contender to poll creates a marker and returns from `acquire()` too. F's release finds another inode at the path (`_unlink_open_marker`) and leaves it. Neither holder learns anything.  Step 4 needs a poll inside one 4 ms tick, and step 5 a second poll inside F's 75 µs gap. Step 5 is far likelier than independent 50 ms timers would make it, because contenders that wait together bunch. With filelock's DEBUG messages timestamped, nine waiters polled within 2 to 3 ms of one another, several 0.1 ms apart or closer. In a run where the other user also recorded what replaced its file, 13 of 100 successors appeared in tick `T`, and a waiter broke 7 of those 13.  `MarkerSoftFileLock` and `SoftFileLease` hand an unparsable marker to the same code, and the lease uses the clock a second time, for expiry: `if owner.mode == "lease" and self._marker_unchanged_for(mtime, ino) >= self._lease_duration: break_lock_file(...)`. `_marker_seen` is one attribute, so the same empty file primes this branch, and step 5 has no gap to hit. To every waiter, F's complete lease record with pair `(T, I)` has gone unrefreshed for `lease_duration`, until F's first heartbeat (the periodic refresh a lease holder runs). With the lock user's processes using `SoftFileLease(path, lease_duration=2)` and holding for 1 s, the same other user produced an overlap in 17 of 30 attempts. The superseded holder's `on_compromise` (the callback that tells a holder it lost the lock) reported `owner-changed` 0.67 s after it had entered, at its first heartbeat; a holder that releases before that is not told at all.  ## Reproduction  The scanner's reproducer for finding `ANT-2026-RKC48J5B`, as received, ran against commit b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1. Attack sequence  ```mermaid sequenceDiagram     participant X as other local user     participant P as lock path (sticky dir, ext4, 4 ms clock ticks)     participant S as process S of the lock user (waiting)     participant F as process F of the lock user     X->>P: create empty file, inode I, utime to future tick T     S->>P: poll: empty file, key (T, I), watch starts     Note over S: after 2 s each poll calls break_lock_file, rename gets EPERM, error swallowed, watch keeps counting     rect rgb(255, 214, 214)         X->>P: at tick T: unlink own file, I is free         F->>P: O_EXCL create in tick T: inode I, mtime T, record not yet written         S->>P: poll: empty file, key (T, I) seen for 2.2 s: break_lock_file(T, I) renames and unlinks F's marker         F->>P: writes record into the unlinked inode, acquire() returns         Note over S,F: the path is empty, the next contender creates a marker: two holders, no error     end ```  ## Evidence  The scanner's reproducer runs ten copies of a default-option `SoftFileLock` program (0.3 s of work per hold, 50 ms between holds) as user `victim` in a root-owned `1777` directory on overlayfs over ext4 (Linux 6.1, CPython 3.14). A program running as user `attacker` waits until the lock path is free, creates an empty file there, dates it to a coarse-clock tick 2.2 to 2.25 s ahead, and unlinks it when `CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE` reaches that tick. Control attempts date the file an hour after the unlink tick (20 attempts, 0 overlaps); the other attempts date it at that tick.  In four runs the overlap came after 9, 12, 27 and 20 attempts. Each showed the hold lines of two `victim` processes overlapping in time with `is_locked=True`, for example `pid=217 entered=241.295272609 exited=241.59542327` and `pid=216 entered=241.295518489 exited=241.595641553`. 40 of 650 attempts over seven runs ended this way, none with the file dated 4 ms earlier (100 attempts) or an hour later (150). A stepped run (one process stalled 0.2 s between creating its marker and writing its record, one waiting contender) deleted the fresh marker in 3 of 3 trials with the matching date and 0 of 5 with other dates.  Our review ran the reproducer over a loop-mounted ext4 `/tmp` (the host's btrfs does not hand a freed number back) with inode reuse confirmed (inode 18 reused on every attempt, `--cpus 2`). 0 of 250 attempts fired on 4.2.0 in 802 s, as in the scanner-side triage, and 0 of 250 on the head of #843, so our run gives no evidence either way. The review confirmed that `utime` cannot set the file's change time. The classification follows from the cross-UID inode-reuse primitive verified in the stale-break race of the separate advisory and from the report's own runs.  ## Impact  A local user who can create a file in a soft lock's directory, a sticky directory such as `/tmp` included, gets two processes of another user to hold the same `SoftFileLock` at once (`MarkerSoftFileLock` too, by the shared code). Neither process learns of the overlap, so both modify the data the lock protects. The other user has no simpler way to get this: in the sticky directory its `unlink`, `rename`, `open(..., "w")` and `utime` on a marker of the lock user all fail, and deleting its own file only frees the lock. For `SoftFileLease` the effect is a live, refreshed claim taken after milliseconds instead of after `lease_duration` without a refresh. The holder learns of it one heartbeat later, or not at all if it releases first. Not affected: releases before 4.1.0, filesystems that do not reuse inode numbers at once (tmpfs, btrfs), and a lock with a single contender.  ## Workarounds  Keep soft locks in a directory other users cannot create files in (a `0700` directory of the lock's user) rather than a shared sticky directory, or put the lock directory on tmpfs, which does not reuse inode numbers. Where the native `FileLock` works (local ext4 with `flock`), prefer it over `SoftFileLock`. Raise `poll_interval` so fewer waiters bunch inside one clock tick; this lowers the hit rate but does not close the window.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) hand SQLite a name they do not control. On Linux the lock validates its database through a descriptor (the number the kernel gives a process for an open file). It then connects SQLite to `/proc/self/fd/<n>`, a Linux path that names the process's own open file `n`. SQLite turns that path back into a plain path and reopens it by name, following symlinks (a symlink is a file that points at another path). On every POSIX route SQLite also acts on `-journal`, `-wal` and `-shm` files it finds beside that name. Those are SQLite's side files: the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write), the write-ahead log or WAL (changes kept outside the main file), and the shared-memory index for the WAL.  Another local user who can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database can turn this against the user running the lock (below: the lock user). Such a directory is a `0777` or group-writable cache, build or project directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). That other user can make the lock user's ordinary `read_lock()` or `write_lock()` write bytes of the other user's choosing into the lock user's own files. The same position lets the other user make that call create or unlink files of the lock user, admit a reader beside a writer, or kill the holder. All of this runs with the lock user's privileges. In a sticky directory such as `/tmp` a planted `-wal` file makes every acquire fail. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 (the `/proc/self/fd` redirect since 4.0.9, the side-file variants since 3.20.4).  Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private as `ANT-2026-KMJ2575J` [high, CWE-363]: ReadWriteLock: SQLite still follows planted symlinks, overwriting files.  ## Severity  **CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H` scores 7.1 (High).** `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): the planted-journal variant needs no race, and the redirect won 77 of 77 attempts. `I:H` (high integrity impact): the other user writes bytes of their choosing into files of the lock user and unlinks files of their choosing. `A:H` (high availability impact): the other user makes every acquire fail or kills the lock holder. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. `S:U` (scope unchanged): the effect stays within the lock user's own privileges.  Classification from the external review: **conditional security**, a cross-user effect that exists only when another user can change names in the lock database's directory. The review notes that the 77/77 inotify result (inotify is a Linux interface that reports file events) is stronger evidence than a theoretical TOCTOU (a time-of-check to time-of-use race). The scanner rated it high. The review accepts the mechanism and narrows it to that precondition.  ## Scope and preconditions  - The other party is a different local account that can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database. That is a `0777` directory or a group-writable one (including a setgid `2775` project directory shared with that account), in each case without the sticky bit. The lock user's lock must be able to open the database read-write, so a database the other user creates is `0666`. filelock itself creates the database `0600`. - Sticky directories (`/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, any `1777` directory) narrow the finding rather than exclude it. The redirect and the journal replay do not reach a database the lock user owns there (tested with `fs.protected_regular=2`). What remains is a planted non-empty `<db>-wal` (any mode; a directory or FIFO works too) that the lock user cannot unlink. It makes every acquire raise `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error`. A hard link (a second name for the same file) to a file of the lock user at the lock path also remains, if `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. - Two kernel settings matter. `fs.protected_regular` (1 or 2 is the systemd default on most distributions; the kernel's own default is 0) keeps a user from opening a file another user owns in a sticky world-writable directory. Where it is 0, the other user can own the database in `/tmp`, and SQLite follows a planted symlink itself (not tested). `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (most distributions; kernel default 0) blocks a hard link of a lock user's file onto the lock path. Neither setting affects a non-sticky shared directory. - Platform and route. The `/proc/self/fd` redirect is Linux with `/proc` mounted, 4.0.9 and later. The side-file variants (`-journal`, `-wal`, `-shm`) exist on every POSIX route. On the hard-link route (macOS since 4.1.1 for every connection, Linux without `/proc`) they need the link-directory swap described under "Mechanism", so a non-sticky parent. Neither the scanner nor the review executed on macOS; the statement rests on the platform branch and the identical code after it. Windows does not take this path. - Ancestor boundary. Protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That holds when each ancestor belongs to the user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename an entry in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.  ## Affected code  At the scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_connect_through_descriptor` builds `/proc/self/fd/<n>` and hands it to `sqlite3.connect`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L982-L1001). The assumption is the [comment at line 63](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L63), "Descriptor paths reopen the validated inode" (an inode is the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name). SQLite first reads the file it opened at [`PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`, line 816](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L816). The check in [`_raise_if_database_replaced` at line 836](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L836) runs only after `BEGIN`. Both [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1091) and [`_raise_if_wal`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1094-L1101) inspect the descriptor, not the file SQLite is on. The one-level hard link of the macOS route is [`_link_beside`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1014-L1029).  ## Introduced  The `/proc/self/fd` redirect came with `4d45e83` ("Merge commit from fork", the fix for GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56), first released in **4.0.9** (verified: `git tag --contains 4d45e83` gives 4.0.9); 4.0.8 does not have it. The side-file variants are older. It checks through the descriptor that the file is a regular file and not a WAL database. It then calls `sqlite3.connect("/proc/self/fd/<n>")` and expects SQLite to reopen the validated inode. An oplock (opportunistic lock) is a request by a process that holds a handle on a file to be told before another process opens, renames or deletes that file; the other process waits until the holder answers the break or closes its handle. The probe also shows that the failed exclusive create and `os.utime` by path return at once, so the wait is in the read and the break, not in the create attempt.  ## Impact  Each `acquire()` of a soft lock that finds a marker another account holds an oplock on runs past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` until the holder answers or closes, 10 s per attempt in the recorded two-account runs. A stale marker under that oplock is not broken, so no process acquires the lock while the holder keeps its handle. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the wait is on the event loop thread and stops every task in the process; with the default executor one worker thread waits. The documentation names a soft lock as the option for network filesystems, after verification on the mount, and `FileLock` is a soft lock on builds without `fcntl` and after its `ENOSYS` fallback. Mutual exclusion is not affected and nothing other than the marker is read, written or deleted.  ## Workarounds  - Keep soft-lock markers in a directory whose ACL grants other accounts no access to new files: a directory inside the user profile, or one with inheritance removed and only the owner, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` granted (`icacls <dir> /inheritance:r /grant:r "<owner>:(OI)(CI)F" "SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F" "Administrators:(OI)(CI)F"`). `mode` does not do this on Windows. - Run `AsyncSoftFileLock` with the default executor rather than `run_in_executor=False`, so that only a worker thread waits. - No `timeout`, `blocking` or `cancel_check` value bounds the wait.  ## Patched version  4.2.1.
